paper.title: Online Detection of Forecast Model Inadequacies Using Forecast Errors
paper.summary: Forecasting models go wrong when the process they forecast changes, and the more complex the model, the harder the change is to spot directly. This paper proposes watching the model's one-step-ahead forecast errors instead, with a sequential changepoint test (Page's CUSUM), whatever the forecasting method. It shows that, when the model keeps a constant bias and cannot fully adapt, a change in the mean or variance of the data appears as a change in the mean of the errors or of their squares, with known limit distributions for the test. Exponential smoothing adapts to mean changes, so with it only variance changes stay visible. In simulations of seasonal data, monitoring forecast errors found changes sooner than monitoring the raw data, with few false alarms. Two examples follow: Royal Mail parcel forecasts and hospital admissions for gallstones.

definitions.definition: A framework that monitors a forecasting model online by applying sequential changepoint detection to its one-step-ahead forecast errors. For a univariate series $Y_t$ and a forecasting model $\mathcal{F}$ with one-step-ahead point forecast $\hat{y}_t(1) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t | y_{t-1}, \ldots, y_1]$, the forecast errors are $$e_t = Y_t - \hat{y}_t(1).$$ The first $m$ forecast errors are the Phase I (training) sample; monitoring starts at $t = m + 1$ and stops when a detector, [[D2:the mean detector]] or [[D3:the squared-error detector]], crosses its threshold. Any forecasting approach can supply the errors: model-based, machine learning or expert judgement.

[[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] applied to the forecast errors of the [[D1:forecast error monitoring framework]]: $$\begin{aligned} Q_\mu(m,k) &= \sum_{t=m+1}^{m+k} e_t - \frac{k}{m} \sum_{t=1}^{m} e_t \\ D_\mu(m,k) &= \max_{0 \le i \le k} \left| Q_\mu(m,k) - Q_\mu(m,i) \right| \end{aligned}$$ with stopping time $$\tau_{\mu,m} = \min\{k \ge 1 : D_\mu(m,k) \ge \hat{\sigma}_{\mu,m} c_{\mu,\alpha} g(m,k,\gamma)\},$$ where $\hat{\sigma}_{\mu,m}$ is the standard deviation of the forecast errors in the Phase I sample. The weight function $g(m,k,\gamma)$ is that of [[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]], and the critical constant $c_{\mu,\alpha}$ comes from the limit distribution of the detector under the null hypothesis.

[[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] applied to the centred squared forecast errors of the [[D1:forecast error monitoring framework]]: $$\begin{aligned} Q_\xi(m,k) &= \sum_{t=m+1}^{m+k} (e_t - \hat{b}_{\mu,m})^2 - \frac{k}{m} \sum_{t=1}^{m} (e_t - \hat{b}_{\mu,m})^2 \\ D_\xi(m,k) &= \max_{0 \le i \le k} \left| Q_\xi(m,k) - Q_\xi(m,i) \right| \end{aligned}$$ with stopping time $$\tau_{\xi,m} = \min\{k \ge 1 : D_\xi(m,k) \ge \hat{\sigma}_{\xi,m} c_{\xi,\alpha} g(m,k,\gamma)\},$$ where $\hat{b}_{\mu,m}$ is the mean of the forecast errors in the $m$ Phase I samples and $\hat{\sigma}_{\xi,m}$ the standard deviation of the centred squared forecast errors in that sample. $g(m,k,\gamma)$ is that of [[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] and $c_{\xi,\alpha}$ comes from the limit distribution of the detector under the null hypothesis. The paper prints the second sum of $Q_\xi(m,k)$ without the square, a typographical error that the guarantor, an author of the paper, has confirmed.

[[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] applied to the raw data instead of forecast errors; for variance changes, to the centred squared raw data. In the paper's simulations its standard deviation $\hat{\sigma}_m$ is the Bartlett long run variance estimator from the sandwich R package.

The detector of the [[D1:forecast error monitoring framework]], [[D2:$D_\mu(m,k)$]] or [[D3:$D_\xi(m,k)$]] by the type of change, applied to the forecast errors of an ARMA forecasting model fitted with the forecast R package. For seasonal data the model is a seasonal ARMA model chosen by auto.arima using AIC, with no differencing. The standard deviation is the traditional estimator, the errors being taken as i.i.d.

The detector of the [[D1:forecast error monitoring framework]], [[D2:$D_\mu(m,k)$]] or [[D3:$D_\xi(m,k)$]] by the type of change, applied to the forecast errors of an ETS forecasting model fitted with the es function of the smooth R package. The standard deviation is the traditional estimator, the errors being taken as i.i.d.
The three detectors compared in the paper's simulations.

A data-generating process with a changepoint at an unknown location $k^*$: $$\begin{aligned} Y_t | y_{t-1}, \ldots, y_1 &\sim F, \quad t = 1, \ldots, m + k^* \\ Y_t | y_{t-1}, \ldots, y_1 &\sim G, \quad t = m + k^* + 1, m + k^* + 2, \ldots \end{aligned}$$ where $F$ and $G$ differ in expectation by $\delta_{\mu,m} \ne 0$. The raw data may be temporally dependent, trended, seasonal or depend on exogenous variables.

The [[D8:mean change model]] extended so that the pre-change distribution $F$ and the post-change distribution $G'$ differ in expectation by $\delta_{\mu,m}$ and in variance by $\delta_{\xi,m}$ (the paper's Definition 1).

The local level exponential smoothing model with additive error, no trend and no seasonality, whose one-step-ahead forecasts follow $$\hat{y}_t(1) = \hat{y}_{t-1}(1) + \alpha e_{t-1},$$ where $e_{t-1}$ is the forecast error at time $t-1$ and $0 < \alpha < 1$ is the smoothing parameter.

A forecasting model for the causal and invertible ARMA($p$,$q$) process $$\phi(B)(Y_t - \lambda_t) = \theta(B)\epsilon_t,$$ with mean parameters $\lambda_t$, autoregressive polynomial $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \cdots - \phi_p B^p$, moving average polynomial $\theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B + \cdots + \theta_q B^q$ and independent zero-mean errors $\epsilon_t$ with variance $\sigma_t^2$.
The mean of the detection delays over the simulated series in which a change was signalled within the length of the data.
The proportion of simulated series in which a change was detected within the length of the monitoring data.
The proportion of simulated series in which a change was detected before the true change had occurred.

Each scenario is simulated 1000 times with normally distributed innovations. Forecasting models are trained on the first $n_{\text{train}} = 300$ observations and then produce one-step-ahead forecasts sequentially. A change is signalled by the theoretical thresholds of [[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] with $\gamma = 0$ and a false alarm rate of 0.05.

Simulated data whose errors follow an ARMA(2,1) model with $\phi = (-0.6, 0.3)$, $\theta = -0.3$, $\lambda = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$, with a mean change of size $\delta_\mu$ at $k^* = 100$ and a seasonal component of frequency 12 whose seasonal means are 12 equally spaced points of $y = 10\sin(x)$, $x \in [0, \pi]$.

Simulated data $y_t = 1[t > m + k^*]\beta t + \epsilon_t$ whose errors follow an ARMA(1,1) model with $\phi = 0.2$, $\theta = 0.2$, $\lambda = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$: no trend before the change and a trend of gradient $\beta$ after it, with a seasonal component of frequency 7 whose seasonal means are 7 equally spaced points of $y = 10\cos(x)$, $x \in [0, 2\pi]$.

Simulated data with AR(1) errors, $\lambda = 0$, whose autoregressive parameter changes at the changepoint from $\phi_{\text{pre}} = 0.2$ (scenario 1) or $\phi_{\text{pre}} = 0.8$ (scenario 2) to varying values $\phi_{\text{post}}$, with quarterly seasonality given by quarter means $(-2, 5, 7, -10)$. The ETS forecasting model is ETS(A,N,A) with estimated smoothing parameters.

Forecast errors of the daily number of parcels to be delivered from one Royal Mail delivery office, from 1 July 2020 to 31 December 2020. The underlying data and forecasts are not known to the authors. July to October is the Phase I sample; monitoring starts on 1 November 2020.

The monthly proportion of A&E admissions related to gallstone-related pathology (GRP) in participating hospitals across England, 2010 to 2020, based on NHS Hospital Episode Statistics. A SARMA(1,0,0)(1,0,0)$_{12}$ model fitted to the data up to 2013 gives one-step-ahead forecasts for the rest; 2013 to 2016 is the Phase I sample of size $m = 36$ and monitoring starts in 2016.
Sequential changepoint detection that fits the model to the data before and after a potential changepoint and decides by a likelihood-ratio style statistic.
The number of observations between a change and the time a detector signals it.
The date of the observation at which a detector first crosses its threshold.

The sequential detector of a mean change in a series $Y_t$ that follows the change in mean model $$Y_t = \begin{cases} \lambda + \epsilon_t, & t = 1, \ldots, m + k^* \\ \lambda + \epsilon_t + \Delta_m, & t = m + k^* + 1, m + k^* + 2, \ldots \end{cases}$$ with zero-mean variables $\epsilon_t$, a training period of length $m$ without changepoints and a change of size $\Delta_m$ at time $k^*$ after it. With $$\begin{aligned} Q(m,k) &= \sum_{t=m+1}^{m+k} Y_t - \frac{k}{m} \sum_{t=1}^{m} Y_t \\ D(m,k) &= \max_{0 \le i \le k} \left| Q(m,k) - Q(m,i) \right| \end{aligned}$$ the null hypothesis $H_0: \Delta_m = 0$ is rejected in favour of $H_A: \Delta_m \ne 0$ at the stopping time $$\tau_m = \min\{k \ge 1 : D(m,k) \ge \hat{\sigma}_m c_\alpha g(m,k,\gamma)\},$$ where $\hat{\sigma}_m$ is a weakly consistent estimator, from the $m$ training samples, of the constant $\sigma$ of the weak invariance principle, the weight function is $$g(m,k,\gamma) = \sqrt{m}\left(1 + \frac{k}{m}\right)\left(\frac{k}{m+k}\right)^{\gamma}, \quad \gamma \in [0, 1/2).$$ and the critical value $c_\alpha$ is taken from the limit distribution under $H_0$, so that $\lim_{m\to\infty} P(\tau_m < \infty) = \alpha$ under $H_0$ for the chosen false alarm rate $\alpha$ and $\lim_{m\to\infty} P(\tau_m < \infty) = 1$ under $H_A$. All limits are for $m \to \infty$; the model is trained once and not re-trained during monitoring. The paper takes $\gamma = 0$.

claims.statement: Under [[D8:the mean change model]], the one-step-ahead forecast errors of a forecasting model that satisfies the two forecasting-model assumptions have a change in mean of size $\Delta_{\mu,m} \ne 0$ at the changepoint: $e_t = b_\mu + \epsilon_{\mu,t}$ for $t \le m + k^*$ and $e_t = b_\mu + \epsilon_{\mu,t} + \Delta_{\mu,m}$ afterwards.

about.subject: D3
about.relation: detects variance changes with

conditions: variance change sizes satisfying Assumptions C to E of the paper's Supporting Information

relations.note: The closest result found: Inclán and Tiao (1994) detect variance changes from the centred squared data; the claim applies the idea to the squared forecast errors of an ETS model.

claims.statement: The forecasting model has a constant bias before the changepoint: $\mathbb{E}_F[Y_t|\tilde{y}_t] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t|\tilde{y}_t] = b_\mu$ for $t = 1, \ldots, m + k^*$, where $b_\mu$ is unknown and may be zero (the paper's Assumption 1, the constant-bias assumption).

After the changepoint the forecasting model does not fully adjust to the change: $$\mathbb{E}_G[Y_t|\tilde{y}_t] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t|\tilde{y}_t] = b_\mu + \Delta_{\mu,m}$$ for $t = m + k^* + 1, m + k^* + 2, \ldots$, where $\Delta_{\mu,m} \ne 0$ is a function of the change size in the raw data (the paper's Assumption 2, the incomplete-adjustment assumption).

The zero-mean variables $\epsilon_t$ of the monitored series, here $\epsilon_{\mu,t}$ and $\epsilon_{\xi,t}$ left in the forecast errors after the bias is removed, satisfy the weak invariance principle of Assumptions A and B of the paper's Supporting Information: $\left|\sum_{t=1}^{m} \epsilon_t\right| = O_P(\sqrt{m})$, and there are Wiener processes $\{W_m(i) : i \ge 0, m \ge 1\}$ and a constant $\sigma > 0$ with $$\sup_{1/m \le i < \infty} \frac{1}{(mi)^{1/\nu}} \left| \sum_{t=m+1}^{m+mi} \epsilon_t - \sigma W_m(mi) \right| = O_P(1) \quad \text{for some } \nu > 2$$.

The change is large enough and bounded: the changepoint is $k^* = \lfloor \theta m^\beta \rfloor$ for some $\theta > 0$ and $0 \le \beta < 1$, $\sqrt{m}\,|\Delta_m| \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$, and $\Delta_m = O(1)$, where $\Delta_m$ is the change size in the monitored series, here $\Delta_{\mu,m}$ or $\Delta_{\xi,m}$, as Assumptions C to E of the paper's Supporting Information require.

The ARMA process is causal and invertible, $\phi(x) \ne 0$ and $\theta(x) \ne 0$ for all $|x| \le 1$, and the ARMA forecasting model is perfectly estimated, so that its residuals and forecast errors are identical.

For [[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] under the null hypothesis of no change, $$\lim_{m\to\infty} P\left(\frac{1}{\hat{\sigma}_m} \sup_{1 \le k < \infty} \frac{D(m,k)}{g(m,k,\gamma)} \le c\right) = P\left(\sup_{0<i<1} \sup_{0 \le j \le i} \frac{1}{i^\gamma} \left| W(i) - \frac{1-i}{1-j} W(j) \right| \le c\right)$$ for every real $c$, where $\{W(i) : i \in [0,1]\}$ is a standard Brownian motion (Theorem 1 of the paper's Supporting Information, from Fremdt 2015).

claims.statement: For [[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] under the alternative of a mean change, $$\lim_{m\to\infty} P\left(\frac{\tau_m - a_m(c_\alpha)}{b_m(c_\alpha)} \le x\right) = \Psi(x)$$ for every real $x$, where $a_m(c)$ is the unique solution of $$a_m(c) = \left(\frac{\sigma c\, m^{1/2-\gamma}}{|\Delta_m|} + \frac{k^*}{(a_m(c))^\gamma}\right)^{1/(1-\gamma)},$$ $$b_m(c) = \frac{\sigma \sqrt{a_m(c)}}{|\Delta_m|} \left(1 - \gamma\left(1 - \frac{k^*}{a_m(c)}\right)\right)^{-1},$$ and $\Psi(x) = 1 - \tilde{\Psi}(-x)$ with $\tilde{\Psi}(x)$ equal to $\Phi(x)$ when $\tilde{\Delta}_m = |\Delta_m| m^{\beta(1-\gamma)-1/2+\gamma} \to 0$, to $P(\sup_{d<i<1} W(i) \le x)$ when $\tilde{\Delta}_m \to \tilde{C} \in (0,\infty)$, and to $P(\sup_{0<i<1} W(i) \le x)$ when $\tilde{\Delta}_m \to \infty$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function, $W$ a standard Brownian motion and $d = d(c)$ the unique solution of $d = 1 - \frac{c}{C} d^{1-\gamma}$ with $C = \theta^{1-\gamma}\tilde{C}$ (Theorem 2 of the paper's Supporting Information, from Fremdt 2014).

evidence.description: Derivation of the mean change in the forecast errors from the two forecasting-model assumptions (Section 2.1 of the paper).

steps.statement: Before the changepoint, $$\mathbb{E}_F[e_t] = \mathbb{E}_F[Y_t|\tilde{y}_t] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t|\tilde{y}_t] = b_\mu,$$ so $e_t = b_\mu + \epsilon_{\mu,t}$ with $\epsilon_{\mu,t}$ of zero mean.
After the changepoint, $\mathbb{E}_G[e_t] = b_\mu + \Delta_{\mu,m}$, so $e_t = b_\mu + \epsilon_{\mu,t} + \Delta_{\mu,m}$ with $\Delta_{\mu,m} \ne 0$.

evidence.description: Proof of Proposition 1 of the paper: the change size of the centred squared forecast errors.

steps.statement: $$\Delta_{\xi,m} = \mathbb{E}_{G'}[(e_t - b_\mu)^2] - \mathbb{E}_F[(e_t - b_\mu)^2],$$ the difference between the post-change and pre-change expectations of the centred squared forecast errors.

With $\delta_{\mu,m} = 0$, substituting $e_t = Y_t - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t] = \mathbb{E}_F[Y_t] - b_\mu$ gives $\Delta_{\xi,m} = \mathrm{Var}_{G'}[Y_t] - \mathrm{Var}_F[Y_t]$.

With $\delta_{\mu,m} \ne 0$, substituting $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[Y_t] = \mathbb{E}_G[Y_t] - b_\mu - \Delta_{\mu,m}$ after the change gives $\Delta_{\xi,m} = \mathrm{Var}_G[Y_t] - \mathrm{Var}_F[Y_t] + \Delta_{\mu,m}^2$.

evidence.description: Corollary 1 and Proposition 2 of the paper: the limit distributions of the squared-error detector follow from Proposition 1 and from Theorems 1 and 2 of the paper's Supporting Information, the limit theory of Page's CUSUM.

steps.statement: The centred squared forecast errors follow a mean change model with change size $\Delta_{\xi,m}$ and zero-mean errors $\epsilon_{\xi,t}$.
Under the null hypothesis the limit distribution of Theorem 1 of the Supporting Information holds with $D(m,k) = D_\xi(m,k)$ and $\hat{\sigma}_m = \hat{\sigma}_{\xi,m}$.

Under the alternative, with $\Delta_{\xi,m}$ satisfying Assumptions C to E, the limit distribution of Theorem 2 of the Supporting Information holds with $\tau_m = \tau_{\xi,m}$ and $c_\alpha = c_{\xi,\alpha}$.

steps.statement: The forecast error after the changepoint is written by repeated substitution of the previous forecast errors into $\hat{y}_t(1) = \hat{y}_{t-1}(1) + \alpha e_{t-1}$ until the pre-change regime is reached, which gives the stated expectation.
As $s$ increases the expectation returns to zero when $\alpha > 0$, and faster for larger $\alpha$, so no constant change $\Delta_{\mu,m} \ne 0$ remains.

evidence.description: Corollaries 1 and 2 of the paper's Supporting Information: the limit distributions of the mean detector follow from the mean change in the forecast errors and from Theorems 1 and 2.

steps.statement: The forecast errors follow the change in mean model of [[D24:Page's CUSUM detector]] with $\lambda = b_\mu$, $\Delta_m = \Delta_{\mu,m}$ and zero-mean errors $\epsilon_{\mu,t}$.
Under the null hypothesis the limit distribution of Theorem 1 holds with $D(m,k) = D_\mu(m,k)$ and $\hat{\sigma}_m = \hat{\sigma}_{\mu,m}$.
Under the alternative, with $\Delta_{\mu,m}$ satisfying Assumptions C to E, the limit distribution of Theorem 2 holds with $\tau_m = \tau_{\mu,m}$ and $c_\alpha = c_{\mu,\alpha}$.

warrants.text: The variance-change formula of Proposition 1 needs only the constant-bias assumption, which an ETS forecasting model can satisfy, so a variance change in the raw data gives a mean change in its squared forecast errors; the limit distributions of the squared-error detector then apply. The mean of the forecast errors themselves returns to zero after a mean change, so only the variance change remains detectable.

A model-based sequential detector must fit the post-change model, here a SARMA(1,0,0)(1,0,0) model with a 12-month season, which the paper states needs at least two years of data after the change; the detectors on the forecast errors signalled four and two observations after it.

limitations.statement: Forecasting models that adapt to a change in mean, such as ETS models with a positive smoothing parameter, do not satisfy the incomplete-adjustment assumption, so a mean change does not stay in their forecast errors.
The two forecasting-model assumptions that make the thresholds theoretically valid are not necessarily satisfied in all the simulated scenarios.
All simulated data have an ARMA error structure with normally distributed innovations and a training sample of 300 observations.

The start of the Christmas peak season at the delivery office is inferred from the rise in the mean and variance of the forecast errors; the underlying parcel volumes and forecasts are not known to the authors.
The application uses one monthly series with a Phase I sample of 36 observations.

open_questions.question: Whether a multivariate sequential changepoint algorithm on the vector of forecast errors of several variables or products detects changes, and how it should treat the sparsity of a change, is left as future work.
How to combine the information in forecast errors from several forecast horizons, beyond the one-step-ahead errors studied, is not established.
